name: Nitrazepam (Mogadon)
summary: Longer-lasting benzodiazepine sleep medication for short-term insomnia. Can work within 20–50 minutes, but the next-day “hangover” and dependence risk are real—this is not an every-night, long-term sleep fix.
description: Nitrazepam (Mogadon) is a benzodiazepine hypnotic used short-term for insomnia (trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early). It can help you get to sleep, but because it lasts a long time, it can also leave you groggy the next day. It can cause memory gaps, falls, and dangerous breathing suppression—especially with alcohol, opioids, or sleep apnea. Use only when safer options have failed, and keep it short (generally days, not months).
patient_summary: Nitrazepam (Mogadon) is a benzodiazepine sleep med used short-term for insomnia. It can work fast (20–50 minutes), but it also lasts long—so next-day grogginess is common. It can be habit-forming, and stopping suddenly after regular use can trigger rebound insomnia and withdrawal. Never combine with alcohol or opioids, and avoid if you have significant sleep apnea or severe liver disease.

linked_conditions.context: Used short-term for insomnia characterized by trouble falling asleep, frequent awakenings, and/or early morning awakenings—typically when safer options (CBT-I, sleep hygiene, non-benzodiazepine strategies) have failed or aren’t available.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to nitrazepam, benzodiazepines, or any component of the formulation
Severe respiratory insufficiency (including clinically significant sleep apnea syndrome)
Use as a hypnotic in children

efficacy_response.patient_text: Nitrazepam can help with sleep onset and sleep maintenance in the short term, but it’s not a best-choice long-term insomnia plan because of next-day impairment and dependence risk. If your insomnia isn’t improving after about 7–10 nights, that’s a sign you need a deeper evaluation—not a stronger sleep pill.

pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Intermediate-acting (classification based on half-life range of ~12-40 hours)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic nitroreduction and acetylation; no active metabolites

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Nitrazepam (Mogadon) is used for short-term insomnia when the problem is serious enough to impair daytime functioning and safer treatments haven’t worked. Because this is a benzodiazepine, it comes with real risks: next-day impairment, falls, memory problems, and dependence—so it’s not meant to be a nightly long-term solution.
items: {link:condition:insomnia:Insomnia}: Trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up too early—short-term use only

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s brain reacts differently, but these are the patterns people tend to describe—especially with a longer-lasting benzo sleep med like this:

quotes: My body finally stopped fighting sleep.
It didn’t knock me out instantly—more like the edge came off and sleep showed up.
I went from wired to sleepy in under an hour.
I slept through the night, but I paid for it the next morning.
Less waking up at 3 a.m.—but I felt heavy when I woke up.
It helped my sleep maintenance… and also made me slow the next day.
items.note: Because nitrazepam has a long half-life, “sleep help” can turn into “next-day fog,” especially if you don’t get a full 7–8 hours in bed.

quotes: I felt like my brain was running on low battery the next day.
Groggy, clumsy, kind of out of it until noon.
It worked, but I couldn’t drive the next morning without feeling sketchy.
items.note: Next-day impairment risk is a major reason benzodiazepines are not first-line insomnia treatments.

quotes: I didn’t remember conversations after I took it.
I woke up and realized I’d eaten at night and barely remembered it.
Dreams got strange—sometimes darker, sometimes just… off.
items.note: Amnesia and complex sleep-related behaviors can happen with benzodiazepines—treat that as a serious warning sign.

quotes: After a couple weeks, it didn’t hit the same.
If I skipped it, my sleep bounced back worse.
It helped, but I could feel my body getting used to it.
items.note: Regular use increases tolerance and dependence risk. This is why most guidance limits use to short stretches, not months.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Nitrazepam can start working within 20–50 minutes, but it lasts a long time. That’s the double-edged sword: it may help you stay asleep, but it can also cause next-day grogginess, slower reaction time, and impaired judgment.
key_points: 20–50 minutes: You may start feeling sleepy
~3 hours: Peak blood levels (strongest effects can be later than you expect)
30 hours: Average half-life (can be longer in older adults)
Next-day impairment: More likely than with shorter-acting sleep meds—especially if you don’t get 7–8 uninterrupted hours

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Nitrazepam can reduce time to fall asleep and improve sleep maintenance in the short term. The problem is the cost: it’s a benzodiazepine with dependence risk and a long half-life, which increases next-day impairment. If insomnia persists beyond about a week or two, the better move is reassessment and treating the underlying driver (anxiety, depression, sleep apnea, circadian issues, meds/substances), plus CBT-I—not just continuing a benzo.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Avoid alcohol and be extremely cautious with opioids—this combo can suppress breathing and can be fatal.
sections.black_box: Benzodiazepines combined with opioids or other sedatives can cause severe sedation, dangerously slow breathing, coma, and death. Avoid the combination when possible and use the lowest dose for the shortest time if there is no alternative.
other: Not a first-line insomnia treatment due to next-day impairment, tolerance, and dependence risk
Limit use to short-term courses; long-term use (over ~4 weeks) should be rare and only when benefits clearly outweigh risks and safer therapies are not available or not effective
Avoid in clinically significant sleep apnea or severe respiratory disease (risk of respiratory depression)
Avoid use in people with current or significant history of substance use disorder or medication misuse
Use caution in depression, especially if suicidal risk is present (can worsen mood or disinhibit behavior in some patients)
Higher fall and injury risk—especially in older adults
patient_counseling: Plan for 7–8 uninterrupted hours of sleep after taking a dose. If you can’t, don’t take it.
If you take opioids or other sedatives, tell your prescriber—this may need to be avoided entirely.
Don’t drive, operate machinery, or make high-stakes decisions until you know how you react the next day.
If you notice memory gaps, unusual nighttime behaviors (sleep-eating, sleep-driving), or agitation, stop and contact a clinician urgently.
If insomnia isn’t improving after 7–10 days, you need reevaluation—not just continuing the medication.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: sedation, next-day grogginess (“hangover”), dizziness, impaired coordination, and memory problems. Like other benzodiazepines, it can also cause paradoxical agitation or disinhibition in some people.
plain_language_list: Dizziness, slowed reaction time, impaired coordination (fall risk)

common.patient_note: This is the expected effect—but with nitrazepam, it can spill into the next day because the medication lasts a long time. If you’re drowsy the next morning, that’s not you being weak. That’s the pharmacology.
Grogginess, slowed thinking, clumsiness, and reduced reaction time can persist into the next day—especially in older adults or if you didn’t get a full 7–8 hours of sleep.
Balance and coordination can take a hit. Falls are a real risk—especially at night when you get up to use the bathroom.
You may not form memories normally for a period after taking it. If you’re having memory gaps, that’s a red flag for dose sensitivity or over-sedation.
Some people describe darker dreams, vivid dreaming, or nightmares. If it’s distressing, this may not be the right med for you.

serious: Respiratory depression (especially with opioids, alcohol, sleep apnea, COPD): slow or shallow breathing, blue lips, unresponsiveness. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis/angioedema): swelling of face/lips/tongue, trouble breathing. MEDICAL EMERGENCY. Do not rechallenge after angioedema.
Paradoxical reactions: agitation, aggression, disinhibition, inappropriate behavior. Stop and seek urgent care.
Complex sleep-related behaviors (sleep-driving, sleep-eating, making calls while asleep): discontinue and seek medical advice urgently.
Worsening depression or suicidal thoughts: treat seriously and contact a clinician immediately.
Withdrawal syndrome after abrupt stopping: rebound insomnia/anxiety, tremor, delirium, rigidity, severe symptoms in rare cases—taper instead of stopping suddenly.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Nitrazepam is a sedating benzodiazepine and is also affected by CYP3A4 interactions. The biggest danger is additive sedation and breathing suppression when it’s combined with other depressants.

items.with: Opioids (including prescription pain meds and illicit opioids)
items.risk: High risk of severe sedation and respiratory depression; can be fatal.
items.action: Avoid when possible. If there is no alternative, use the lowest effective doses for the shortest time and monitor closely.

items.risk: Synergistic CNS depression: profound sedation, impaired breathing, blackouts, falls, death.
items.action: Do not combine. Zero alcohol while this is in your system.

items.with: Other CNS depressants (sleep meds, sedating antihistamines, muscle relaxants, antipsychotics, gabapentinoids, cannabis)
items.risk: Additive impairment: oversedation, confusion, falls, memory issues, impaired driving.
items.action: Avoid stacking sedatives. If combination is unavoidable, reduce doses and monitor for next-day impairment and breathing problems.

items.risk: May raise benzodiazepine exposure and increase sedation and impairment.
items.action: Dose adjustment or avoidance may be needed; review interactions before prescribing.

items.with: CYP3A4 inducers (certain seizure meds, rifampin, herbal products like St. John’s wort)
items.risk: May lower levels and reduce effect—or trigger withdrawal symptoms in dependent patients.
items.action: Avoid if possible; reassess sleep strategy rather than escalating benzodiazepine dosing.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been taking nitrazepam regularly, do not stop abruptly. Even when the goal is “just for sleep,” the brain can adapt to benzodiazepines, and stopping suddenly can trigger rebound insomnia and withdrawal symptoms.
key_points: Suggested taper: Reduce by 25% of the original dose every 1–2 weeks until the lowest available dose is reached, then discontinue.
If you’ve been on it longer-term or you’ve tried and failed to stop before: go slower and pair the taper with CBT-I (cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia).
Expect rebound insomnia for 1–2 days in some people after stopping GABAergic sleep meds; severe withdrawal is uncommon but can happen after sustained use or big dose drops.
Avoid abrupt discontinuation; monitor for withdrawal symptoms (anxiety, irritability, tremor, sweating, nausea, agitation, worsening sleep).

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Nitrazepam is typically taken at bedtime, as needed, for short-term insomnia. Because it can cause next-day impairment and dependence, it’s usually reserved for cases where safer options have failed.

adult.sleep_initial: 5 to 10 mg PO once at bedtime as needed
adult.prn_use: Use at bedtime as needed; generally limit to short-term use (often 7–10 consecutive nights) and reassess if ongoing use is considered
adult.elderly: Avoid use when possible. If used: 2.5 mg PO at bedtime as needed; may increase to 5 mg at bedtime if tolerated (maximum 5 mg/day)
adult.hepatic: Mild-to-moderate impairment: no specific adjustment provided; use with caution. Severe impairment: contraindicated
adult.renal: No specific adjustment provided; use with caution

sections.simple_explanation: This is a longer-lasting benzodiazepine, so it may help you stay asleep—but that longer duration also increases the chance you’ll feel impaired the next day. The goal is the lowest effective bedtime dose for the shortest possible time.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Nitrazepam isn’t a go-to option in pregnancy, breastfeeding, or older adulthood because the risks can outweigh the benefits—especially when there are safer insomnia treatments available. If it’s being considered anyway, it should be a careful, individualized decision.
sections.pregnancy: Nitrazepam crosses the placenta. In-utero benzodiazepine exposure may be associated with fetal risk, and late-pregnancy exposure can cause neonatal sedation and/or withdrawal symptoms. For insomnia in pregnancy, nonpharmacologic treatment (like CBT-I) is preferred first. If medication is considered, the plan should be individualized with risk-benefit discussion and close monitoring.
sections.lactation: Nitrazepam is present in breast milk, and infant sedation or poor feeding has been reported with benzodiazepines in case reports. Breastfeeding is not recommended by the manufacturer. If exposure occurs, monitor the infant for sedation, irritability, and feeding/weight changes, keeping in mind the long half-life and potential accumulation.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid in adults 65+ when possible. Benzodiazepines increase risk of impaired cognition, delirium, falls, fractures, and motor vehicle accidents. If used despite risks, start at the lowest dose (2.5 mg at bedtime as needed) and do not exceed 5 mg/day; reassess frequently and discontinue as soon as feasible.
sections.hepatic: Use with caution in mild-to-moderate hepatic impairment. Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment.
sections.renal: No formal adjustment provided; use with caution due to increased sensitivity and risk of accumulation-related impairment in some patients.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Next-day impairment: grogginess, slowed reaction time, cognitive fog—especially important for driving safety
Falls and balance: especially in older adults or anyone getting up at night
Respiratory status: higher risk in sleep apnea, COPD, or when combined with other sedatives/opioids
Mental status: confusion, disorientation, memory issues, unusual behavior
Mood: worsening depression, irritability, emotional lability, suicidal ideation
Signs of tolerance/dependence: escalating dose needs, “can’t sleep without it,” withdrawal or rebound insomnia when missed
Medication interactions: review sedatives and CYP3A4-related interactions before starting or adjusting
Cardiovascular status if clinically indicated: hypotension, palpitations (rare but reported)

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: In Canada, nitrazepam is available as oral tablets. Tablets can be swallowed, crushed, or dissolved in liquid. For insomnia, it’s taken at bedtime.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Nitrazepam is a benzodiazepine that boosts the effect of GABA—the brain’s main calming signal—by binding to benzodiazepine sites on the GABA-A receptor complex. That increases inhibitory signaling (think: more braking in the nervous system), which can reduce arousal and make sleep more likely. It does not act on GABA-B receptors.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: For insomnia, nitrazepam is not a first-line choice. The first-line treatment is CBT-I (cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia) plus sleep scheduling and stimulus control. Benzodiazepines are generally reserved for short-term, severe cases where safer options have failed or aren’t available—and even then, the plan should be time-limited, lowest dose, and reassessed quickly. It’s a particularly cautious choice in older adults because of falls, cognitive effects, and higher overall harm.

seo.title: Nitrazepam (Mogadon): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects & Withdrawal
seo.description: Nitrazepam (Mogadon) for short-term insomnia: bedtime dosing (5–10 mg), how fast it works (20–50 min), next-day grogginess risk, dependence/withdrawal, dangerous interactions (alcohol/opioids), and safe tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Nitrazepam is used for short-term treatment of insomnia—trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early—when the sleep problem is impairing daytime functioning and safer options haven’t worked.

faqs.q: How fast does nitrazepam work for sleep?
faqs.a: Many people feel it within about 20–50 minutes. Peak levels are later (around 3 hours), so the strongest effects may build over the first part of the night.

faqs.q: Why do people feel groggy the next day on nitrazepam?
faqs.a: Because it lasts a long time. Nitrazepam’s half-life is around 30 hours (often longer in older adults), so the sedating effects can carry into the next day—slowing reaction time, attention, and coordination.

faqs.q: What’s a typical dose for insomnia?
faqs.a: Adults usually take 5 to 10 mg by mouth at bedtime as needed. In older or debilitated adults, it’s generally avoided—but if used, dosing is lower: 2.5 mg at bedtime as needed, up to 5 mg max.

faqs.q: Can I take nitrazepam every night long-term?
faqs.a: Usually no. Benzodiazepines can cause tolerance, dependence, and next-day impairment. Most guidance keeps use short-term (often 7–10 consecutive days), with reassessment if it continues beyond 2–3 weeks.
It can be. Like other benzodiazepines, it can cause tolerance and physical dependence—especially with regular use. That’s why it’s meant to be time-limited and carefully monitored.

faqs.q: How do I stop nitrazepam safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been taking it regularly, don’t stop abruptly. A common approach is reducing by 25% of the original dose every 1–2 weeks until the lowest dose is reached, then stopping. People on long-term therapy often need a slower taper, ideally paired with CBT-I.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol if I take nitrazepam?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol plus a benzodiazepine is a dangerous combination that can cause severe sedation, blackouts, falls, and suppressed breathing. It can be fatal.

This is high-risk. Opioids plus benzodiazepines can suppress breathing and increase overdose risk. The safest approach is to avoid the combination unless there’s no alternative and it’s closely monitored.

faqs.q: Is nitrazepam safe if I have sleep apnea?
faqs.a: If you have clinically significant sleep apnea, nitrazepam is generally a bad idea because benzodiazepines can suppress respiratory drive and worsen breathing during sleep. This is especially important if you also use other sedatives.

faqs.q: Is nitrazepam a good choice if I’m depressed?
faqs.a: Often no. In depression—especially if suicidal risk is present—benzodiazepines can sometimes worsen mood, reduce inhibition, or increase risk. If it’s used at all, it should be time-limited and carefully supervised.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: Sedation, next-day grogginess (“hangover”), dizziness, impaired coordination, and memory problems. Some people also report vivid dreams or nightmares.

faqs.q: Is nitrazepam available in the United States?
faqs.a: No—nitrazepam is not available in the U.S. market. Availability and brand names vary by country.
